lessons.title: What Counts as Salary for HRA: Basic Pay, DA and Commission

body.text: In the HRA formula, "salary" is not what lands in your bank account. It is a short list of three items. Getting that list right can move your exemption by lakhs, and adding more to salary does not always help.

children.text: Ask ten colleagues what salary means for HRA and you will hear gross pay, CTC, take-home and basic. Only one of those is close. Rule 279 of the Income-tax Rules, 2026, which sets the limits for the exemption under Schedule III (Table: S. No. 11) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (Rule 2A and Section 10(13A) under the old law), uses a deliberately narrow definition. Since salary appears in two of the three limits, a wrong figure makes your whole calculation wrong.

markDefs.definition: For the HRA calculation: basic pay, plus dearness allowance if the terms of employment provide for it, plus commission paid as a fixed percentage of turnover achieved by the employee. All other allowances and perquisites are excluded.

children.text: means basic pay, plus dearness allowance if your terms of employment provide for it, plus commission paid as a fixed percentage of turnover you achieve. Rule 279 expressly excludes every other allowance and perquisite. It is also measured as salary due for the relevant period, the months you lived in the rented home.

children.text: Basic Pay: The Number Doing Most of the Work

For most private-sector employees, salary for HRA is simply basic pay, because they receive no DA and no turnover commission. That makes your basic the most important figure in the calculation. It also means your basic is set by your employer's pay structure, not by tax law.

body.label: Why basic pay has been rising
body.value: Wages at least 50% of total remuneration
body.context: Under the Labour Codes in force since 21 November 2025, basic, DA and retaining allowance must make up at least half of pay. Many employers raised basic, which changes salary for HRA even when CTC is unchanged.

children.text: Dearness Allowance: Mostly a Government and PSU Item

Dearness allowance compensates for inflation. It is standard for central and state government employees, PSUs, banks and many aided schools and colleges, and rare in private companies. When your terms of employment provide for DA, it is part of salary for HRA.

This central government employee's HRA in an X-class city is 30% of basic only, ₹13,470 a month, because pay commission HRA is not calculated on DA. But the tax calculation uses basic plus DA as salary, ₹71,840. Two different "salaries" for two different purposes on the same payslip.

body.text: Some payroll software and blogs describe the DA test as "DA forming part of retirement benefits", which is the test used for gratuity and leave encashment. Rule 279 asks whether your terms of employment provide for DA. For most government and PSU employees both tests give the same answer, but if your DA is unusual, check your appointment letter or service rules.

children.text: Sales roles often carry commission. In Gestetner Duplicators (Pvt.) Ltd. v. CIT, decided in 1978, the Supreme Court held that commission paid under the employment contract at a fixed percentage of turnover achieved by the employee is part of salary. That principle is still applied to HRA. Commission that is discretionary, a flat amount or tied to company-wide results does not meet it.

body.title: Quick Check: Which Payment Is Salary?
body.question: Deepak is a medical representative in Lucknow. Which of these payments counts as salary for his HRA calculation?
options: A ₹25,000 Diwali bonus paid to all sales staff
A 2% commission on the sales he personally achieves, as set out in his appointment letter
A one-time incentive for beating the regional target, decided by his manager
body.explanation: Only commission at a fixed percentage of the turnover he achieves, under his terms of employment, is included. The Diwali bonus and target incentive are not turnover-linked commission, and the field allowance is an allowance, which Rule 279 excludes.

children.text: More Salary Is Not Always Better

Here is the part most people miss. Salary sits in Limit 2 with a minus sign and in Limit 3 with a plus sign. So adding an item to salary, or getting a higher basic, can raise or lower your exemption depending on which limit binds.

body.latex: \text{Extra exemption per extra rupee of salary} =\begin{cases} -0.10 & \text{if Limit 2 binds} \\ +0.50 \text{ or } +0.40 & \text{if Limit 3 binds} \\ 0 & \text{if Limit 1 binds} \end{cases}
body.caption: Holding HRA and rent constant. A large change can shift which limit binds.

body.title: The facts behind Rahul and Farah

children.text: Rahul is a sales executive in Ahmedabad (50% city). Basic ₹30,000 a month, HRA ₹15,000 a month, rent ₹18,000 a month, and 3% commission on the ₹40 lakh of sales he achieved. Commission adds ₹1,20,000 to salary. Limit 2 falls by ₹12,000, and because Limit 2 is now the smallest, his exemption drops from ₹1,80,000 to ₹1,68,000. Leaving commission out would overstate his exemption, which is exactly the kind of error a tax officer corrects.

Farah works for a Jaipur cooperative bank (40% city). Basic ₹40,000 a month, DA ₹10,000 a month under her service rules, HRA ₹20,000 a month, rent ₹30,000 a month. Leaving DA out, Limit 3 is the smallest at ₹1,92,000. Including DA raises Limit 3 to ₹2,40,000, which is now tied with Limit 1, so her correct exemption is ₹2,40,000, ₹48,000 higher. Her payroll team had been under-claiming for her.

body.text: The right salary figure is not a planning choice. You cannot leave commission out to get a bigger exemption, or add a bonus to get one. The definition is fixed. What you can do is check that your employer applied it correctly in both directions.

body.title: Scenario: The Labour Code Restructure in Mumbai
body.scenario: Nikhil works for a media company in Mumbai and pays ₹45,000 a month rent in Andheri. His old structure: basic ₹40,000, HRA ₹20,000 (50% of basic), special allowance ₹60,000. After his employer restructures for the Labour Codes, his CTC is unchanged, but basic becomes ₹60,000, HRA ₹30,000 and special allowance ₹30,000. He is on the old regime, in the 30% slab, with no DA or commission.
body.prompt: What happens to his annual exempt HRA and to his tax? Is there any catch?
body.modelAnswer: Before: salary ₹4,80,000; Limit 1 ₹2,40,000; Limit 2 ₹5,40,000 minus ₹48,000 = ₹4,92,000; Limit 3 ₹2,40,000. Exempt HRA ₹2,40,000. After: salary ₹7,20,000; Limit 1 ₹3,60,000; Limit 2 ₹5,40,000 minus ₹72,000 = ₹4,68,000; Limit 3 ₹3,60,000. Exempt HRA ₹3,60,000. His exemption rises by ₹1,20,000, because both Limit 1 and Limit 3 grew with his basic while his high rent kept Limit 2 out of the way. Money moved out of fully taxable special allowance and into basic and HRA, so his taxable salary falls by ₹1,20,000, saving about ₹37,440 a year at 30% plus cess. The catch: if his employer calculates PF at 12% of his full basic, his PF contribution rises by ₹2,400 a month, or ₹28,800 a year. That money is still his, in his PF account, and can count towards Section 80C, but his monthly take-home pay falls.

body.title: Try It: Lakshmi in Chennai
body.prompt: Lakshmi teaches at an aided college in Chennai. Her basic pay is ₹35,000 a month, her DA is ₹14,000 a month under her service rules, her HRA is ₹12,000 a month and she pays ₹14,000 a month in rent. She is on the old regime. What is her annual exempt HRA? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: Salary includes DA: (₹35,000 + ₹14,000) × 12 = ₹5,88,000. Limit 1: ₹1,44,000. Limit 2: ₹1,68,000 minus ₹58,800 = ₹1,09,200. Limit 3: 50% of ₹5,88,000 = ₹2,94,000. The smallest is Limit 2, so ₹1,09,200 is exempt. If DA had been wrongly left out, Limit 2 would be ₹1,26,000 and the exemption would be overstated by ₹16,800.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Minus Sign
body.textWithBlank: When Limit 2 is your binding limit, every extra ₹1,000 of salary for HRA reduces your exemption by ₹___.
body.explanation: Limit 2 is rent minus 10% of salary. An extra ₹1,000 of salary adds ₹100 to the amount subtracted, so Limit 2, and your exemption, fall by ₹100, as long as Limit 2 stays the smallest.

body.title: Build Your "Salary for HRA"
steps: Take your monthly basic from your payslip
Check your appointment letter or service rules. If they provide for DA, add your DA
If you earn commission, check whether it is a fixed percentage of turnover you achieve. If yes, add the commission for the period
Ignore every other line on the payslip, including HRA, special allowance, bonus and reimbursements
Multiply by the number of months you lived in the rented home, using the actual figures for each month if they changed
Compare your figure with the salary your employer used in its HRA working, and ask HR to explain any difference

cards.definition: Basic pay plus DA if the terms of employment provide for it plus commission at a fixed percentage of turnover achieved. Everything else is excluded.
An inflation-linked allowance common in government, PSU and bank jobs. Counts as salary for HRA when the terms of employment provide for it.
Commission at a fixed percentage of the sales an employee achieves under the employment contract. Treated as salary following the Supreme Court's Gestetner Duplicators ruling.
Salary is measured for the period it relates to, the months you occupied the rented home, not simply when it was paid.
If Limit 2 binds, each extra ₹1 of salary cuts the exemption by 10 paise. If Limit 3 binds, it adds 50 or 40 paise. If Limit 1 binds, nothing changes.

points: Salary for HRA is only basic pay, DA provided by your terms of employment, and commission at a fixed percentage of turnover
HRA, special allowance, bonus, perquisites and employer PF contributions are all excluded
For most private-sector employees, salary for HRA is simply basic, so salary restructuring under the Labour Codes directly changes it
Government and PSU employees must include DA, now 60% of basic for central government staff from January 2026
A higher salary lowers the exemption when Limit 2 binds and raises it when Limit 3 binds, so getting the definition wrong can cut either way
The definition is fixed by law, so the goal is to check that your employer applied it correctly, not to choose what to include
